title: Italian town carries towering Virgin Mary structure through streets
content:
Thousands of residents and visitors converged on the historic town of Sora in central Italy on August 15 to take part in the annual Feast of the Assumption. The centerpiece of the celebration was a 16‑metre‑high illuminated structure, known locally as the “candelora,” which was carried on the shoulders of devotees as they paraded through the narrow, cobbled streets. Local authorities coordinated traffic diversions and safety measures, allowing the procession to move uninterrupted while ensuring the crowd’s security.

The tradition, which dates back several centuries, marks the Catholic observance of the Virgin Mary’s assumption into heaven and is a focal point of communal identity in Sora. The towering, brightly lit monument, adorned with candles and religious symbols, was lifted at dawn and guided by a procession of volunteers, musicians, and clergy, culminating in a mass held at the town’s main cathedral. Organizers said the event reinforced cultural heritage and fostered social cohesion, drawing participants from neighboring villages and attracting media attention. The celebration concluded with fireworks, leaving the town poised to repeat the ritual in the years ahead.
author: Euronews

title: No toilets, no shelter, little protection. In Ceuta, DW finds thousands of minors living alone on the streets.
content:
Several thousand unaccompanied minors have gathered in Ceuta, the Spanish enclave on the northern coast of Africa, where authorities report a surge in illness and abuse among the children. The influx has overwhelmed local shelters and medical facilities, prompting officials to admit that the current capacity is insufficient to meet the urgent needs of the vulnerable population.

Health workers have documented widespread cases of respiratory infections, dehydration, and psychological distress, while reports of physical and verbal abuse have emerged from both residents and humanitarian groups. The Spanish government has called for additional resources and coordination with international partners, but the sheer volume of children and the limited infrastructure have stalled effective response efforts.

The situation remains critical as Ceuta’s authorities continue to manage the crisis, highlighting the urgent need for expanded support and long‑term solutions to protect the rights and well‑being of the unaccompanied minors.
author: DW World

title: Libya: Drone Strike Sets Oil Refinery Ablaze Amid Election Stalemate
content:
The United Nations Security Council convened to review Libya’s escalating crisis, where a stalled political process has postponed planned elections and intensified armed clashes. The meeting also addressed recent drone attacks that set fire to a major oil refinery, further destabilising the country’s already fragile infrastructure.

During the session, an activist highlighted how the convergence of extreme heat, water scarcity, and environmental shocks with political fragmentation, armed conflict and weak institutions creates a complex peace‑and‑security challenge. The council urged urgent measures to address both the immediate security threats and the underlying governance gaps that hinder Libya’s recovery.

The council’s deliberations underscore the urgency of a coordinated international response to restore stability, secure critical infrastructure, and pave the way for a credible electoral process in Libya.
author: UN News

title: UN experts urge Singapore to halt death penalty for drug offenses
content:
Independent experts appointed by the United Nations Human Rights Council condemned the execution of at least 16 individuals in Singapore this year, all of whom were convicted of drug‑related offences. The experts described the use of capital punishment in the country as “continued and unlawful” and called on Singapore to halt the death penalty in all cases.

Singapore maintains that its death‑penalty regime is a necessary deterrent against drug trafficking, a crime that the government views as a serious threat to public safety. The country has carried out a total of 16 executions since the start of the year, a figure that has drawn criticism from international human‑rights bodies. The UN experts urged the Singaporean authorities to review their legal framework and align it with global standards that increasingly view the death penalty as a violation of fundamental human rights.

In response to the condemnation, Singapore has reiterated its commitment to its existing laws, citing the need to protect citizens and uphold national security. The UN call for reform highlights the growing international pressure on Singapore to reconsider its stance on capital punishment and to explore alternative sentencing options for drug‑related crimes.
author: UN News

title: Only 3% of Gaza's cropland remains usable for farming
content:
Amid the continuing violence in Gaza, farmers are confronting a growing crisis of land security as they attempt to cultivate crops. The region’s agricultural sector, already strained by limited arable land, is now facing additional obstacles from shelling, unexploded ordnance, and the displacement of communities that have traditionally relied on small plots for subsistence and income.

Local authorities report that many fields lie in areas of active conflict or near military checkpoints, making it dangerous for workers to enter. In addition, the destruction of irrigation infrastructure and the lack of reliable water supply further hinder productive farming. Efforts by humanitarian groups to map safe zones and provide protective measures have met with limited success, as the dynamic front lines and sporadic airstrikes continue to shift the boundaries of what can be considered secure for agricultural activity.

The situation underscores the broader impact of the conflict on civilian livelihoods. While international agencies are coordinating emergency food assistance, the long‑term viability of Gaza’s agricultural economy remains uncertain until hostilities subside and the region can restore stable, safe land for cultivation.
author: UN News

title: UN expands aid for 100,000 people after Colombia earthquake
content:
The United Nations announced on Tuesday that it is expanding its humanitarian response in western Colombia as the region grapples with escalating needs following a 7.4‑magnitude earthquake that struck the area last week. The latest update from the UN detailed plans to increase the delivery of emergency supplies, medical services, and temporary shelter to communities most affected by the tremor, which caused widespread damage to homes, infrastructure and local livelihoods.

The scaling‑up of assistance comes as local authorities report a growing number of displaced families and heightened demand for basic necessities. UN agencies are coordinating with Colombian government bodies and non‑governmental partners to streamline aid distribution and to assess ongoing gaps in relief efforts. Officials indicated that the expanded operation will remain in place until the immediate humanitarian situation stabilizes, underscoring the UN’s commitment to supporting the affected population in the coming weeks.
author: UN News

title: Leg Strength Declines Three Times Faster Than Muscle Mass in Adults Aged 70‑79, Study Shows
content:
Researchers have uncovered a striking pattern in the aging process that challenges common assumptions about muscle health. A three‑year longitudinal study followed nearly 1,900 adults aged 70 to 79, tracking both muscle mass and strength. Even among participants who maintained or increased their muscle mass, the data revealed a consistent decline in muscular strength, with leg strength dropping at a rate roughly three times faster than the loss of muscle tissue.

The study employed regular assessments of lean body mass via dual‑energy X‑ray absorptiometry and functional strength tests, including leg press and grip strength measurements. While overall muscle mass decreased modestly across the cohort, the rate of strength loss was disproportionately steep, particularly in the lower limbs. These findings suggest that factors beyond sheer muscle quantity—such as neuromuscular coordination, tendon elasticity, and metabolic efficiency—play a crucial role in preserving functional capacity among older adults.

The implications for public health and exercise prescription are significant. Strength training programs that focus solely on building muscle mass may not fully address the rapid decline in functional strength observed in aging populations. Future interventions might need to incorporate neuromuscular and functional components to better maintain independence and quality of life in older adults.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Spain builds tent cities for the thousands stuck in Ceuta
content:
Spain is constructing four temporary reception sites in Ceuta, with a total capacity of 1,500 places, to accommodate the estimated 5,000 migrants currently housed in the Spanish enclave. The new facilities aim to improve living conditions and streamline the processing of arrivals, which have surged in recent months.

The temporary sites will provide basic accommodation, medical care, and administrative support, allowing authorities to better manage the influx and reduce overcrowding in existing shelters. Officials say the expansion is part of a broader strategy to address the humanitarian and logistical challenges posed by the high number of migrants awaiting processing.

Once operational, the sites are expected to relieve pressure on Ceuta’s current infrastructure and help ensure that migrants receive timely assistance while their status is determined. The Spanish government will monitor the situation closely as the new facilities become active.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Disney Sues FCC Over ABC Station Renewal
content:
The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) is under increased scrutiny after the Walt Disney Company publicly challenged a renewal order it received for the ABC broadcast network’s license. Disney argues that the FCC’s decision is driven by political motives aimed at penalizing ABC for its coverage of recent political events, rather than being based on the agency’s regulatory criteria. The company claims that the FCC’s actions are retaliatory and violate the principles of fair and impartial oversight.

In the renewal hearing, the FCC cited several technical and compliance issues that it said warranted a stricter licensing framework for ABC. Disney, however, contends that these concerns are overstated and that the real intent behind the order is to curb ABC’s reporting on politically sensitive topics. The dispute has drawn attention from both media watchdogs and political commentators, who are monitoring whether the FCC’s regulatory process remains free from partisan influence. The FCC has stated that its decision was made in accordance with established guidelines and that it remains open to further review.

The outcome of this conflict could set a precedent for how broadcast licenses are evaluated in politically charged contexts. If the FCC’s renewal order stands, it may signal a shift toward more stringent oversight of major networks. Conversely, a reversal or modification of the order could reinforce the agency’s commitment to neutrality. The case remains closely watched as it touches on the broader debate over media regulation and political influence in the United States.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Iran Prepares to Sustain Economy Amid US Sanction Threats
content:
Iran’s senior officials have warned that the country could move to offensive military operations if Washington pursues additional sanctions. The statement, issued by the Iranian foreign ministry, comes amid a renewed U.S. effort to tighten restrictions on Iran’s nuclear program, oil exports and financial transactions. The Iranian government cited the potential economic and diplomatic fallout from new sanctions as a catalyst for a more assertive posture.

In the briefing, the ministry said that any escalation would be “measured and targeted” and would focus on protecting Iran’s national interests and regional stability. Officials noted that the U.S. has already imposed a series of punitive measures over the past year, including limits on Iranian oil sales and a crackdown on entities linked to Iran’s ballistic missile program. They added that the Iranian military is preparing contingency plans to respond to what it perceives as an increasingly hostile environment.

The warning underscores the growing tension between Tehran and Washington as the U.S. considers expanding its sanctions regime. While Iran has historically maintained a policy of deterrence, the new threat of offensive action signals a shift in its strategic calculus. The U.S. has indicated that it will weigh the economic impact on Iran against the broader goal of curbing nuclear proliferation, leaving the next phase of the dispute uncertain.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Nigerian influencer arrested after $28 million cocaine seizure bound for UK
content:
Afolabi Kazeem Micheal, a businessman known for his involvement in import‑export operations, has been named in a series of allegations that connect him to an international drug‑trafficking network. Law enforcement agencies in several jurisdictions have reportedly linked his name to shipments intercepted in transit ports, suggesting a possible role in the distribution chain. Despite repeated requests for comment, Michela has not responded to inquiries from the press or the authorities overseeing the investigation.

Officials from the coordinated task force handling the case have declined to disclose further specifics, citing the ongoing nature of the probe and the need to protect the integrity of the investigation. No formal charges have been filed against Michela at this stage, and he remains a person of interest pending additional evidence. The situation continues to develop as authorities pursue leads across multiple countries.
author: BBC World

title: Disney and ABC sue FCC to block early license renewal
content:
The network has formally accused the current administration of engaging in retaliatory actions against the ABC broadcasting company, alleging that the government’s measures are driven by displeasure with the content aired by the network. In a statement released Monday, the network claimed that recent regulatory pressures, licensing reviews, and the withholding of certain public funds constitute a targeted response to ABC’s editorial choices, which the administration reportedly "disapproves of what ABC broadcasts."

The administration has not yet responded to the allegations, and officials have declined to comment on the specific accusations. Observers note that the dispute unfolds amid broader tensions between media outlets and government authorities over press freedom and the role of public broadcasting. The outcome of any investigations or legal challenges could have implications for the regulatory environment governing broadcasters in the country.
author: BBC World

title: Pakistan court orders former PM Imran Khan's transfer to hospital
content:
Former Pakistani prime minister Imran Khan has remained in custody since his arrest in 2023 on multiple corruption allegations, including accusations of misusing state resources and illicit financial dealings. The charges stem from investigations conducted by the National Accountability Bureau, which allege that Khan and associates benefited from irregular contracts and foreign donations while he held office. Legal proceedings have progressed through the Islamabad trial courts, where the former leader has been denied bail on several occasions, extending his detention pending a final verdict.

Khan and his Pakistan Tehreek‑e‑Insaf (PTI) party maintain that the case is politically motivated, asserting that the prosecution is part of a broader effort to sideline a popular opposition figure ahead of upcoming elections. International human‑rights groups have called for a transparent judicial process, while domestic political analysts note that the imprisonment could reshape Pakistan’s political landscape by limiting PTI’s mobilization capacity. The court’s forthcoming decision will determine whether Khan’s incarceration continues or if he will be released pending appeal, a development that will likely influence both domestic stability and regional diplomatic dynamics.
author: BBC World

title: TikTok voicemaxxing trend among young men does not impress women
content:
TikTok has become a hotbed for lifestyle‑optimization challenges, with new trends emerging that promise to boost everything from appearance to nutrition. Among the most popular are “Looksmaxxing,” which offers tips for enhancing physical attractiveness; “Fibermaxxing,” which encourages increased dietary fiber intake for digestive health; “Proteinmaxxing,” a regimen focused on maximizing protein consumption to support muscle growth; and “T‑maxxing,” a trend that encourages users to adopt a “time‑maximization” strategy for productivity. Each trend is typically promoted through short, visually engaging videos that combine expert advice, before‑and‑after transformations, and user testimonials.

The rapid spread of these challenges is fueled by TikTok’s algorithm, which favors content that elicits high engagement and shares. Influencers and everyday users alike post step‑by‑step guides, product recommendations, and personal progress updates, often using branded hashtags to create a sense of community. While some participants report tangible benefits—such as improved sleep patterns, increased muscle tone, or better digestion—health professionals caution that many of the claims lack rigorous scientific backing and that overemphasis on quick fixes can lead to unhealthy behaviors or unrealistic expectations.

Despite these concerns, the trend underscores a growing appetite for self‑improvement content on social media. As TikTok continues to expand its reach, platforms and regulators are monitoring the potential health implications of viral lifestyle hacks. For now, users are encouraged to approach these trends critically, seeking evidence‑based guidance before making significant changes to their diet or routine.
author: Phys.org

title: Minors living alone on Ceuta's streets at risk of abuse
content:
Thousands of unaccompanied minors have gathered in Ceuta, the Spanish enclave on the northern coast of Africa, where authorities report that the influx is overwhelming local resources. The children, many of whom arrived from sub‑Saharan Africa and the Middle East, are now facing widespread illness and abuse, according to statements from the Spanish government and humanitarian organizations operating in the region.

Spanish officials have acknowledged that the current capacity of Ceuta’s reception centers is insufficient to meet the demand, citing shortages of medical supplies, adequate shelter, and trained staff. Human rights groups have called for an urgent increase in international aid and a coordinated response that includes improved screening, health checks, and protection measures against exploitation. The situation has drawn criticism from both local and international actors, who argue that the lack of infrastructure is exacerbating the vulnerability of the children.

The Spanish government has pledged to expand temporary accommodation and to enhance medical support, while also seeking additional funding from the European Union and partner NGOs. Meanwhile, the international community remains on alert, urging a comprehensive strategy to address the humanitarian crisis and to ensure the safety and well‑being of the minors awaiting processing in Ceuta.
author: DW World

title: Iranian League Begins After US-Israel Conflict Escalates
content:
Tehran – In the wake of the escalating conflict that began after the United States and Israel launched coordinated strikes against Iranian targets earlier this month, the Iranian Premier League resumed operations with its opening fixture held last week. The match, scheduled for April 20, 2026, marked the first professional football game in the country since the hostilities commenced, and was conducted under heightened security protocols approved by the Ministry of Sports and the national security apparatus.

The contest featured defending champions Persepolis FC against longtime rivals Esteghlal Tehran, ending in a 2‑1 victory for Persepolis after a tightly contested first half and a decisive goal in the 78th minute. Attendance was limited to 15,000 spectators, roughly half the stadium’s capacity, following directives to minimize potential risks. Officials noted that the match proceeded without incident, and the league’s governing body affirmed its commitment to maintaining the season’s schedule while monitoring the broader security situation.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Brazil President Lula celebrates oil discovery near Amazon River
content:
Environmentalists have lodged strong objections to a new exploratory drilling operation being conducted in the offshore waters at the mouth of the Amazon River. The project, initiated by PetroBrasil Energy in partnership with an international consortium, marks the first offshore hydrocarbon exploration in a region known for its extensive mangrove forests, rich biodiversity and the proximity of several indigenous fishing communities.

The critics, represented by the Amazon Coastal Alliance and the Global Marine Conservation Network, argue that seismic testing and drilling pose risks of oil spills, disruption of marine habitats and long‑term damage to the river’s ecological balance. Government officials from Brazil’s National Agency of Petroleum, Natural Gas and Biofuels (ANP) confirmed that the activity is proceeding under a temporary permit pending a comprehensive environmental impact assessment, and they have pledged to monitor compliance with mitigation measures. The agencies involved have scheduled a public hearing for next month to review the findings and determine whether the exploratory phase will be extended, modified, or halted.
author: BBC World

title: Scientists investigate non-neuronal mechanisms of thought and their AI implications
content:
Researchers are revisiting the long‑standing question of whether biological memory is fundamentally distinct from the way computers store and retrieve data. Recent experiments have highlighted how a familiar song can instantly evoke a memory from decades ago, how a particular scent can summon a specific person or place, and how a frightening recollection can trigger an almost immediate emotional and physical reaction. These observations underscore the powerful role of sensory cues in human memory retrieval.

Neuroscientists are now comparing these biological mechanisms with computational models that rely on pattern recognition and associative networks. While computers can store vast amounts of information and retrieve it based on input patterns, the human brain’s ability to link memories to multi‑sensory experiences and to produce rapid, automatic responses remains a key area of inquiry. Studies employing functional imaging and machine learning are probing whether artificial systems can mimic the same depth of contextual binding that characterizes human memory.

The implications of this research extend beyond basic science. Understanding the parallels and differences between biological and computational memory could inform the design of more intuitive human‑computer interfaces, improve memory‑assisting technologies for patients with cognitive impairments, and guide ethical considerations in artificial intelligence. As the field advances, scientists anticipate clearer insights into how memory functions across living and artificial systems.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Kent Beck publishes article on composable tests
content:
Kent Beck, a veteran software engineer and pioneer of Test‑Driven Development, recently released a short newsletter titled “Composable Tests.” The article, available on his personal newsletter site, has drawn attention on Hacker News, where it has accumulated 15 points and one comment. Beck’s piece focuses on a testing paradigm that encourages building tests from reusable, composable components rather than monolithic, ad‑hoc test suites.

In the newsletter, Beck explains that composable tests treat each test as a small, independent unit that can be combined with others to create more complex scenarios. By modularizing test logic, developers can reduce duplication, improve maintainability, and accelerate refactoring. He also outlines practical guidelines for implementing composable tests in existing codebases, including how to structure helper functions, manage state, and integrate with continuous‑integration pipelines. The discussion touches on the benefits of clearer test intent and the potential for automated test generation when components are well‑defined.

The piece has sparked a modest but focused conversation on Hacker News, with readers praising the clarity of the concepts and questioning how best to transition legacy projects to a composable testing approach. While the discussion remains brief, Beck’s insights contribute to an ongoing dialogue about modern testing practices and the evolution of quality assurance in software development.
author: Hacker News

title: Migrant children on Ceuta's streets risk abuse, exploitation
content:
Thousands of unaccompanied minors have congregated in Ceuta, a Spanish autonomous city on the northern coast of Africa, creating a severe humanitarian and logistical crisis. Local officials have acknowledged that the rapid influx has exceeded the capacity of existing reception infrastructure, prompting urgent requests for coordinated regional and international assistance. The situation has drawn scrutiny from migration authorities and human rights monitors as administrative systems struggle to process and shelter the growing population.

Reports from health workers and aid organizations indicate that many of the minors are suffering from untreated illnesses and have endured physical and psychological abuse during their transit. Overcrowded temporary shelters, limited medical supplies, and inadequate sanitation have compounded the health risks, while authorities admit they lack the personnel and funding to provide comprehensive care. Spanish and Moroccan agencies, alongside European migration bodies, are working to register the children, deliver emergency medical services, and establish legal pathways for their protection, though bureaucratic delays and resource shortages continue to hinder operations.

As the crisis unfolds, officials stress the necessity of sustained cross-border cooperation and increased financial support to safeguard the minors' immediate well-being. Temporary facilities are being expanded, and procedural frameworks for handling unaccompanied migrants are under review to improve long-term management. The gathering in Ceuta highlights ongoing structural challenges facing European border regions in balancing migration control with international protection obligations.
author: DW World

title: New Gaza Working Groups Tie Reconstruction to Immediate Disarmament
content:
The United Nations and a coalition of donor states have announced the creation of a series of “Gaza Reconstruction Working Groups” that will coordinate the delivery of humanitarian aid and the rebuilding of infrastructure in the strip after the recent cease‑fire. The groups, chaired by senior officials from the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) and the World Bank, are designed to streamline funding, logistics, and technical assistance across sectors such as water, electricity, housing, and health. Their mandate is to establish a unified reconstruction strategy that can be implemented once hostilities cease and the area is secured.

A key stipulation attached to the funding and operational support is the immediate disarmament of armed groups operating in Gaza, most notably Hamas. The condition, outlined in a joint statement by the United States, the European Union, and the United Nations, requires that all weapons caches be surrendered and that security forces be restructured under an internationally monitored framework. Supporters argue that disarmament is essential to prevent future conflict and to safeguard the reconstruction process, while critics warn that the requirement could delay aid and exacerbate humanitarian needs. The working groups will monitor compliance through a joint oversight committee that will report progress to the donor community and the UN Security Council.

If the disarmament condition is met, the reconstruction teams will begin work within weeks, targeting critical infrastructure such as the Gaza Strip’s electricity grid, water supply, and damaged residential areas. The international community has pledged up to $15 billion in aid, contingent on the successful implementation of the disarmament agreement. The outcome of this initiative will shape the pace and scope of Gaza’s post‑conflict recovery, with implications for regional stability and the broader peace process.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Hakainde Hichilema wins second term as Zambia president
content:
Zambia’s president, Hakainde Hichilema, has entered his second term amid a fragile economic recovery that many observers say will determine whether his administration can deliver substantive change for the country’s citizens.  The 2024 elections saw Hichilema secure a decisive victory over his predecessor, with voters hopeful that his pro‑market reforms and anti‑corruption agenda would translate into tangible improvements in living standards.

The new administration faces a complex mix of challenges: a high debt burden, persistent inflation, and a need to diversify an economy that remains heavily reliant on copper exports.  Hichilema’s government has pledged to boost investment in infrastructure, education, and healthcare, while also implementing fiscal consolidation measures to restore investor confidence.  Whether these policies can translate into real economic growth and job creation will be closely watched by both domestic stakeholders and international lenders.

Ultimately, Hichilema’s second term will be judged by the pace and breadth of Zambia’s economic turnaround.  If the recovery delivers higher wages, reduced poverty, and stronger public services, it could cement his legacy as a transformative leader; if not, the promise of change may remain unfulfilled.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Alaska and Wyoming primaries highlight Republican leadership shifts
content:
Republican‑led states are undergoing a series of leadership changes as governors and legislative leaders announce new appointments and resignations across a range of agencies. In Texas, Governor Greg Abbott named a former state judge to head the Department of Criminal Justice, while Florida’s Senate Majority Leader announced a retirement that will trigger a caucus vote to select a successor. Similar moves have been reported in Ohio, where the governor’s office confirmed a reshuffle of the health department’s senior staff, and in North Carolina, where the lieutenant governor’s office appointed a new chief of staff. The announcements, issued over the past week, cite routine transitions, retirements and the desire to align agency leadership with evolving policy priorities.

These adjustments come as Republican majorities in several state legislatures prepare for upcoming budget cycles and the 2026 midterm elections, prompting officials to position experienced administrators in key roles. State officials emphasize that the changes are intended to maintain continuity of services and to support the implementation of ongoing initiatives in areas such as public safety, health care and infrastructure. Observers note that the reshuffling may influence the strategic direction of state policies, though the immediate impact will depend on the speed of the transitions and the priorities set by the newly appointed leaders.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Gas prices rise as some drivers pay nearly $7 per gallon
content:
Some drivers in the United States are now paying almost $7.00 per gallon for gasoline, a level that has pushed the average retail price above the $6.50 mark that was reached last month. According to the latest data from the American Automobile Association, the spike is most pronounced in the Midwest and the South, where several major refineries have reported increased operating costs and supply constraints. The rise follows a sharp rebound in crude oil prices, which have climbed by more than 20 percent over the past six weeks, and the ongoing impact of seasonal demand as summer travel ramps up.

Fuel‑price analysts point to a combination of factors that are driving the surge. Higher crude prices are being passed on to consumers, while refinery maintenance schedules and occasional shutdowns have reduced domestic output. In addition, the U.S. Department of Energy’s recent announcement of a temporary fuel tax exemption for electric vehicles has shifted some consumer spending toward gasoline, further tightening the market. State regulators are monitoring the situation closely, and several governors have called for a review of the current fuel pricing structure to ensure that consumers are not unduly burdened.

As the summer travel season continues, gasoline prices are expected to remain volatile. Industry experts advise drivers to plan routes that avoid high‑traffic corridors and to consider alternative transportation options where possible. The Department of Transportation has pledged to keep a close eye on market conditions and to coordinate with federal agencies to address any supply disruptions that could further elevate fuel costs.
author: The Hill

title: Deus Ex creator Warren Spector announces retirement from game development
content:
Warren Spector, the visionary behind landmark titles such as *Deus Ex* and *System Shock*, has announced his retirement from game development. The decision, reported by *Video Games Chronicle*, comes after a career spanning more than three decades during which Spector helped shape the narrative and design standards of modern interactive entertainment.

Spector’s departure follows a period of reflection on the changing industry landscape and the personal toll of constant innovation. In his statement, he noted that the creative drive that once fueled his projects has diminished, and he prefers to focus on other pursuits outside of game design. The announcement has prompted discussion among industry veterans and fans alike, with the article drawing 21 points and three comments on a related discussion thread.

The gaming community will miss Spector’s distinctive blend of storytelling and player agency, but his legacy endures through the enduring influence of his titles and the many developers he has inspired. His retirement marks the end of an era for a creator whose work set a benchmark for immersive, choice‑driven gameplay.
author: Hacker News

title: Japanese Activist Continues Protests Against Israel's Gaza Genocide
content:
Japanese activist Yuki Sato has continued to stage public demonstrations in Tokyo calling Israel’s military operations in Gaza “genocide.”  The protests, which began in early 2024, have included a series of street rallies, a petition signed by more than 5,000 residents, and a televised interview in which Sato urged the Japanese government to impose diplomatic sanctions on Israel.  The activist has also distributed informational leaflets at major transit hubs, citing United Nations reports that document civilian casualties and alleged war crimes.

Sato’s campaign follows a broader international outcry over the Gaza conflict, which has seen intensified air strikes and a blockade that has cut off essential supplies to the Strip.  The Japanese government has maintained a position of neutrality, calling for a ceasefire while refusing to label the situation as genocide.  In response, Sato has organized a monthly “Peace March” that draws a diverse crowd, including students, veterans, and local NGOs, all of whom have called for an immediate halt to hostilities and for humanitarian aid to reach civilians.

The activist’s persistence has drawn attention from both domestic and foreign media.  While her efforts have not yet shifted Japan’s official stance, they have amplified public debate on the humanitarian impact of the Gaza war.  Sato remains committed to her advocacy, planning additional demonstrations in the coming months as the conflict continues to evolve.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Wassim al-Assad Sentenced to Death for Syrian War Atrocities
content:
A Syrian court sentenced Wassim al‑Assad to a term of imprisonment on Thursday, marking the second high‑profile verdict issued in recent days against members of the former ruling family. The 15‑year jail term, handed down by the Damascus Civil Court, follows charges of embezzlement and illicit enrichment tied to contracts awarded during the regime’s final years in power. Prosecutors presented evidence that Wassim, a cousin of the deposed president, had overseen a network of state‑owned enterprises that diverted public funds into private accounts, a claim the defense disputed but did not successfully refute.

The judgment arrives just one week after an opposition tribunal in the city of Idlib sentenced ousted President Bashar al‑Assad to death for crimes against humanity, including the use of chemical weapons and the suppression of civilian protests. International observers have noted the rapid succession of these rulings as part of a broader effort by Syrian opposition groups to hold former officials accountable amid ongoing negotiations over the country’s political future. Both sentences underscore the heightened legal scrutiny facing the Assad family as the nation seeks a transitional framework and reconciliation process.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Palestinian-American confronts Israeli settler in Qusra village
content:
A Palestinian‑American man identified as Loui Abu Ridi confronted an Israeli settler at the settler’s residence in the West Bank village of Qusra, located south of Nablus. The encounter, reported by local sources, took place within the contested area where Israeli settlements and Palestinian communities coexist amid ongoing tensions.

Authorities have not released further details regarding the circumstances of the confrontation or any subsequent actions taken by security forces. The incident adds to a series of recent reports of friction between settlers and residents in the region, underscoring the volatile environment that persists in the occupied territories.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Qatar denies Iran claim it is holding missing pilots
content:
Doha – Qatar’s foreign ministry on Tuesday dismissed Tehran’s allegation that Iran is detaining a missing aircrew as “untrue” and a “media ploy,” noting that the Iranian government has not provided any verification of the claim. The statement came after Iranian officials suggested that members of a Qatar‑based flight crew were being held in the country, a charge that Qatar said was unsupported by any evidence and contradicted ongoing diplomatic communications between the two states.

Qatar’s officials emphasized that they have not received any formal notification or request for assistance regarding the alleged detention and that all Qatar‑registered aircraft and personnel continue to operate in accordance with international aviation regulations. The ministry urged the media to refrain from spreading unsubstantiated reports and called for any legitimate concerns to be addressed through established diplomatic channels. No further details about the crew’s identity or the circumstances of their disappearance have been released, and the matter remains unresolved pending verification from Iranian authorities.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Heavy metals may help lung cancer resist chemotherapy

author: Medical Xpress

title: Brunswick Corp. focuses on AI navigation and new revenue as boat sales stall
content:
Brunswick Corp. CEO David Foulkes told CNBC that the company’s premium‑segment boat sales remain robust, even as demand for its value‑priced models continues to lag. In a recent interview, Foulkes highlighted that the high‑end product line, which includes luxury yachts and performance vessels, has sustained a steady sales volume, buoyed by a strong resale market and a loyal customer base.

Foulkes explained that the lag in value‑option sales is largely attributable to broader economic uncertainty and tighter consumer spending, which has made buyers more cautious about higher‑price purchases. He noted that Brunswick’s strategy is to focus on product differentiation and after‑sales service for the premium segment while exploring cost‑effective production techniques to make the value line more competitive.

Looking ahead, Foulkes indicated that Brunswick will continue to invest in research and development to enhance the appeal of its premium offerings and to refine its value‑line pricing strategy. The company’s leadership remains confident that the premium market will sustain growth, while incremental improvements in the value segment could help balance overall sales performance.
author: CNBC Business

title: As temperatures get hotter, pesticides are more dangerous to farmworkers
content:
Recent scientific findings indicate that rising temperatures significantly intensify the health and environmental risks associated with pesticide exposure. Researchers have documented that heat accelerates the chemical breakdown and volatility of common agricultural and residential pesticides, leading to higher concentrations of toxic byproducts in air, soil, and water. This interaction between climate conditions and chemical agents raises concerns for both human populations and ecosystems, particularly in regions experiencing increasingly frequent and prolonged heatwaves.

Studies reveal that elevated temperatures increase the rate at which pesticides volatilize and penetrate biological tissues, while simultaneously impairing the metabolic processes responsible for detoxification. Laboratory and field data show that heat stress can reduce liver and kidney efficiency, making organisms more susceptible to chemical toxicity even at standard application levels. Agricultural workers, communities near treatment zones, and non-target species such as pollinators and aquatic life face compounded risks during high-temperature periods, prompting researchers to recommend revised safety protocols and seasonal application adjustments.

As global temperatures continue to rise, experts emphasize the need for updated regulatory frameworks that account for climate-driven changes in pesticide behavior. Ongoing environmental monitoring and adaptive management strategies are being prioritized to mitigate exposure risks and safeguard public health and ecological stability in warming climates.
author: Ars Technica

title: Gang Leader Ordered Tupac's Murder, Prosecutor Says
content:
Rapper Tupac Shakur was shot dead in an act of gang revenge ordered by a mobster who later boasted of it, jurors heard Monday as one of America’s most anticipated trials opened, 30 years after the murder. The proceedings focus on a former associate of the Los Angeles crime syndicate who is alleged to have directed the hit and subsequently bragged about the killing to friends and associates. The testimony, delivered by law‑enforcement officials and witnesses, details how the mobster allegedly orchestrated the attack and how he later claimed credit for the murder in private conversations.

The case, which has drawn national attention since the 1996 shooting, is expected to shed new light on the circumstances surrounding Shakur’s death. Prosecutors argue that the mobster’s confession and the corroborating evidence establish a clear chain of command from the crime syndicate to the execution of the hit. Defense attorneys counter that the evidence is circumstantial and that the mobster’s statements were made under duress. The trial will continue through the next several weeks, with a verdict expected in the spring.
author: France 24

title: US Cuts Joint Drills with South Korea, Raising North Korea Tensions
content:
The United States announced that it will reduce the size of its joint military exercises with South Korea, a decision that many analysts see as a diplomatic overture toward Pyongyang. The change follows a series of escalations on the Korean Peninsula, including North Korea’s recent missile tests and a surge in rhetoric that has raised concerns about a potential conflict. By scaling back the drills, Washington signals a willingness to ease tensions while maintaining a posture of deterrence.

The decision comes amid a broader strategy to engage North Korea through dialogue and economic incentives. In recent weeks, the North has conducted a series of short-range missile launches and has intensified propaganda campaigns, portraying the U.S. and South Korean forces as a direct threat. The reduction in joint exercises is intended to create a more conducive environment for negotiations, while the U.S. continues to support South Korea’s defense readiness through other security measures.

If the move succeeds, it could open a window for renewed diplomatic talks and a potential easing of sanctions. However, the North’s continued military provocations and its rhetoric suggest that any progress will require sustained pressure and careful management of the security dynamics on the peninsula.
author: DW World

title: Rains aid containment of major Belgium wildfire in High Fens
content:
Firefighters are still battling one of Belgium’s most destructive wildfires, which has scorched an area roughly the size of half Manhattan near the German border. The blaze, which erupted in the early summer, has spread across dense forest and rural farmland, creating a massive smoke plume that has been visible from the capital.

Heavy rains and cooler temperatures that began last week are beginning to slow the fire’s advance, allowing crews to establish containment lines and protect nearby villages. Despite the weather assistance, the fire remains active, with teams working around the clock to prevent it from reaching the border towns and to safeguard wildlife habitats. The incident has prompted a coordinated response from local fire services, the Belgian military, and cross‑border partners in Germany.

While the exact extent of damage is still being assessed, authorities report that the fire has already destroyed several hectares of forest and damaged a handful of homes. As the weather improves, officials expect the situation to stabilize, but they remain cautious, urging residents in the surrounding area to stay alert and to follow evacuation orders if issued.
author: DW World

title: Myanmar revokes Rohingya citizenship, sparking expulsions and ICJ genocide case
content:
Myanmar’s 1982 Citizenship Law, amended in 2015, formally excluded the Rohingya—a predominantly Muslim community in Rakhine State—from the nation’s legal definition of citizenship. The legislation required proof of residence before 1948 and a series of other onerous criteria that the Rohingya could not satisfy, rendering them effectively stateless. In 2017, a military crackdown on alleged insurgent activity triggered a humanitarian crisis, with over 700,000 Rohingya fleeing to Bangladesh and other neighboring countries. The mass expulsions were accompanied by widespread reports of violence, forced displacement, and systematic denial of basic rights, prompting international condemnation and calls for accountability.

In response to these events, Bangladesh filed a genocide case against Myanmar at the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in 2017, alleging that the state’s actions constituted genocide under the Genocide Convention. The ICJ dismissed the case in 2023 on jurisdictional grounds, but the proceedings highlighted the international community’s scrutiny of Myanmar’s citizenship policies and human rights record. The stripping of citizenship has left millions of Rohingya stateless, fueling continued displacement and drawing sustained attention from global legal and humanitarian bodies.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Qatar rejects Iran's claims about missing pilots, citing sovereignty breach
content:
Qatar’s foreign ministry spokesperson, Majed al‑Ansari, announced that Iranian aircraft entered Qatari airspace without authorization, constituting a breach of the nation’s sovereignty. The incursion, which occurred on Thursday morning, prompted Qatari authorities to activate standard defensive protocols, resulting in the interception and escort of the planes out of the country’s airspace. Al‑Ansari emphasized that the response was carried out in full compliance with international aviation law and Qatar’s national security regulations.

The ministry reiterated that any unauthorized aerial activity will be addressed according to established legal frameworks, underscoring Qatar’s commitment to protecting its territorial integrity. No injuries or damage were reported, and diplomatic channels are expected to be used to address the incident with Iran. The episode highlights ongoing regional tensions and the importance of adherence to sovereign airspace rights.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Kariba ferry disaster death toll climbs to 93 in Zimbabwe
content:
Recovery operations are ongoing after the nation’s deadliest transport disaster, which has left more than 100 people dead and dozens injured. Emergency crews, including firefighters, medical personnel, and military units, have been working around the clock to retrieve bodies, treat the wounded, and secure the crash site. The incident, which occurred on a major highway near the capital, involved a passenger bus that collided with a freight truck under hazardous weather conditions, prompting a large‑scale response from local authorities and international aid organizations.

Officials have opened a formal investigation to determine the precise causes of the collision and to assess any systemic safety failures. While the search for survivors has concluded, teams continue to clear debris and provide support to families of the victims. The government has pledged financial assistance for those affected and announced plans to review transport regulations in an effort to prevent a recurrence of such a catastrophic event.
author: BBC World

title: Russia summons Japanese ambassador over PM's anti‑Russian remarks
content:
Russia has summoned Japan’s ambassador to Moscow to protest remarks made by Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, who described Russia as an “anti‑Russian” state in a recent interview. The diplomatic move was announced by the Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, which said the comments were “unacceptable” and demanded an explanation from the Japanese government.

Takaichi’s remarks came amid heightened tensions between the two countries over the ongoing conflict in Ukraine and Japan’s support for sanctions against Russia. The summons follows a series of diplomatic exchanges, including Japan’s earlier statement urging the withdrawal of Russian forces from Ukrainian territory. Moscow’s action signals a firm response to what it perceives as hostile rhetoric from Tokyo, while Japan maintains that it is pursuing a policy of neutrality and diplomatic engagement. The incident underscores the strained relations between the two nations as they navigate competing geopolitical interests in the region.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Study Finds TB Preventive Treatment Reduces Deaths in HIV Patients
content:
Tuberculosis (TB) remains the leading cause of death among people living with HIV, accounting for roughly a quarter of all AIDS‑related fatalities in 2024. Health authorities report that the disease continues to claim more lives than any other single illness in this population, despite the fact that TB is both preventable and curable with standard treatment regimens. The persistence of this trend highlights gaps in early diagnosis, treatment initiation, and adherence among people with HIV.

The World Health Organization and national public‑health agencies attribute the high mortality rate to a combination of factors, including late presentation of TB symptoms, limited access to rapid diagnostic tests, and interruptions in antiretroviral therapy that weaken immune defenses. Efforts to integrate TB screening into routine HIV care, expand drug‑susceptibility testing, and strengthen community‑based treatment support are being intensified in high‑burden regions. However, resource constraints and health‑system fragmentation continue to impede widespread implementation of these strategies.

Addressing the TB‑HIV nexus remains a critical priority for global health initiatives. Continued investment in preventive measures such as isoniazid preventive therapy, improved vaccination coverage, and enhanced public‑health infrastructure is essential to reduce the disproportionate toll of TB on people living with HIV and to move toward the broader goal of eliminating TB as a public‑health threat.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Heatwaves damage Monet's gardens in the North of France
content:
France’s series of heatwaves this year has taken a toll on the country’s horticulture, with the famed gardens of Claude Monet’s Giverny estate among the most visible victims.  The extreme temperatures have stressed plants and livestock across the region, causing wilting, reduced flowering and in some cases outright loss of key specimens that have long attracted visitors from around the world.

At Giverny, the heat has damaged several of the garden’s iconic features, including the water lily pond that once inspired Monet’s celebrated water‑lily paintings and the delicate tulip beds that bloom each spring.  France 2 reporters and horticultural expert Oliver Farry have noted that the sustained high temperatures have accelerated plant senescence, leading to a decline in the health of both ornamental and native species.  The damage is expected to affect the garden’s seasonal displays and may require extensive restoration work before the next tourist season.

The situation underscores the growing vulnerability of France’s cultural and natural heritage to climate extremes.  While restoration efforts are underway, the damage at Giverny serves as a stark reminder of the broader impact of heatwaves on agriculture, horticulture and historic landscapes across the country.
author: France 24

title: Ebola in DRC: Deadliest outbreak on record ‘outpacing the response’
content:
WHO Spokesperson Tarik Jašarević has warned that the full extent of Ebola virus circulation remains unknown, with undetected transmission chains and delayed care significantly hindering containment efforts. In a discussion with Eve Irvine, Jašarević highlighted that many infected individuals are not accessing treatment centers, while patients presenting late face much poorer survival odds. The spokesperson stressed that the inability to locate all active cases creates a critical vulnerability, as hidden transmission continues to drive the outbreak despite ongoing response measures.

author: France 24

title: Russia Intensifies Missile Strikes on Ukraine, Casualties Rise
content:
Families across Ukraine are grieving the loss of soldiers and civilians while Ukrainian military analysts publicly criticize Washington’s failure to deliver on its pledges of advanced weaponry and logistical aid.  The latest wave of casualties, many of whom were killed in recent offensives near Kharkiv and the Donbas region, has intensified the emotional toll on communities already strained by displacement and economic hardship.  In the wake of these losses, a group of senior Ukrainian experts convened in Kyiv to address the gap between the United States’ public commitments and the tangible support that frontline forces require.

The experts cited several high‑profile statements from Washington officials that promised “rapid delivery” of air‑defence systems, precision‑strike weapons, and training programs.  However, shipments have been delayed by bureaucratic hurdles, export‑control restrictions, and shifting priorities within the U.S. Department of Defense.  Analysts noted that the current inventory of supplied equipment falls short of the operational needs identified by Ukrainian commanders, who report that many of the promised systems are still in transit or pending approval.  The gap has led to calls for a reassessment of the aid package and for clearer timelines to ensure that the promised resources reach the frontlines promptly.

In conclusion, the juxtaposition of grieving families and expert criticism underscores a growing frustration among Ukrainian stakeholders.  The nation’s leadership remains hopeful that Washington will expedite the delivery of critical military support, while the emotional weight of loss continues to press the urgency of these demands.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Former gang leader Duane Keffe D Davis begins trial in Tupac Shakur murder case
content:
Former gang boss Duane “Keffe D” Davis is on trial in Las Vegas for the 1996 murder of rapper Tupac Shakur, marking the first prosecution in the decades‑old case. Davis, a former leader of the Southside Crips, was indicted on murder and conspiracy charges after a Clark County grand jury found probable cause based on newly obtained witness testimony and forensic evidence linking him to the drive‑by shooting outside the MGM Grand.

Prosecutors presented a timeline that places Davis at the scene on September 7, 1996, and allege he hired a hitman, citing recorded conversations and a 1996 phone call as key evidence. The defense contended that the case relies on unreliable informants and that the evidence does not meet the burden of proof. The trial has drawn attention from Shakur’s family, who have long sought justice, and from law‑enforcement agencies that have pursued leads for more than three decades.

The verdict will determine whether the first criminal trial in the Tupac Shakur murder brings closure to a high‑profile homicide that has remained unsolved for thirty years and may set a precedent for other cold‑case prosecutions.
author: Al Jazeera

title: The Salt Path film set for U.S. release by Rialto Distribution in September
content:
The feature film *The Salt Path* is set to hit U.S. screens this September under the distribution banner of Rialto Distribution. The company, known for bringing independent and international titles to American audiences, will handle the film’s theatrical release across the country.

*The Salt Path* follows its international premiere schedule, with Rialto’s involvement marking the first official U.S. distribution partnership. The September release date positions the film for late‑summer audiences, and the distributor’s marketing plan will focus on the film’s unique narrative and visual style to attract viewers in major markets.

With the U.S. launch confirmed, fans of the film can anticipate its availability in select theaters nationwide this September, supported by Rialto Distribution’s established network of exhibitors and promotional channels.
author: BBC Entertainment

title: India’s Cockroach movement urges audits of government schools after killing
content:
A group described as the “Cockroach” leadership has called on its supporters to conduct audits of the nearest government‑run schools, citing concerns over mismanagement and alleged corruption. The call, issued through the organization’s official channels, urges members to gather evidence, review financial records, and report irregularities to the appropriate oversight bodies.

The initiative, however, has been marred by violence. Earlier this week, a supporter of the movement was killed during a confrontation at a local school, an incident that has drawn condemnation from both education authorities and human rights observers. Police have launched an investigation into the shooting, and the incident has raised questions about the safety of the audit campaign and the group’s methods.

Authorities have urged calm and called for a thorough, independent inquiry into the killing. While the “Cockroach” group maintains that its audit efforts are aimed at improving transparency, the incident has highlighted the potential risks of politicized oversight initiatives and underscored the need for clear legal frameworks governing such activities.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Officer Noel Pichardo faces multiple internal affairs probes after criticizing city’s Flock cameras
content:
Noel Pichardo, a city official, publicly criticized his municipality’s adoption of Flock surveillance cameras, citing concerns about privacy and community impact. Within a period of less than two years, Pichardo became the subject of five separate internal‑affairs investigations conducted by the city’s oversight unit.

Each inquiry examined alleged misconduct or policy violations connected to Pichardo’s conduct, with the first probe following his public remarks and subsequent investigations triggered by additional incidents reported by the department. The series of investigations underscores the heightened scrutiny faced by officials who challenge the city’s surveillance strategy and reflects the department’s commitment to enforcing internal standards.
author: Wired

title: Lamour Leaves FIFA After Criticising Infantino's World Cup Plan
content:
Kevin Lamour, a former FIFA executive and former head of the FIFA Ethics Committee, publicly criticised a proposal put forward by FIFA President Gianni Infantino last month. In a statement released to the press, Lamour alleged that FIFA staff had been “deceived” over the details of the plan, arguing that the information circulated internally did not accurately reflect the proposal’s scope or implications.

The proposal in question was part of Infantino’s broader agenda to overhaul FIFA’s governance structure, including changes to the composition of the Executive Committee and the introduction of new oversight mechanisms. Lamour, who has long been involved in FIFA’s internal ethics and compliance functions, contended that the staff briefing omitted key aspects of the reforms, thereby misleading employees about the potential impact on decision‑making processes and accountability.

Lamour’s remarks have added a new layer of scrutiny to Infantino’s reform drive. While FIFA has not yet responded formally to the criticism, the comments come at a time when the organization is under pressure to demonstrate transparency and integrity in its governance reforms. The outcome of the debate will likely influence the next steps in the implementation of the proposed changes.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Meta Faces Legal Challenges Over Design and Youth Impact
content:
Meta Platforms Inc. is facing a wave of legal challenges across the United States, the European Union, and other jurisdictions, all centered on the design of its social‑media platforms and their effects on younger users. In the United States, the Federal Trade Commission has sued Meta for alleged deceptive practices that encourage addictive use among minors, while several state attorneys general have pursued claims that the company failed to adequately protect children from harmful content and advertising. In Europe, the European Commission is investigating Meta under the Digital Services Act for potential violations related to algorithmic content curation and the exposure of under‑age users to inappropriate material.

The lawsuits and regulatory inquiries highlight growing concerns about how Meta’s recommendation algorithms, privacy settings, and in‑app features influence the mental health and safety of minors. Meta has responded by pledging to strengthen age verification, improve content moderation, and provide clearer parental controls, but critics argue that these measures fall short of the safeguards required by law. The company’s legal team is also preparing defenses in other markets, including Canada and Australia, where similar complaints about child safety and data privacy have emerged.

If the legal challenges succeed, Meta could face significant fines, mandatory redesigns of its platforms, and stricter oversight of its data practices. The outcome will likely set a precedent for how tech firms manage the balance between user engagement and the protection of vulnerable populations, shaping regulatory approaches worldwide.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Syrian Man Dies in Custody After Alleged Security Abuse
content:
A 38‑year‑old Syrian national, Ahmed Khalid, died while in custody at a police station in Aleppo on Monday, according to his family.  Khalid’s relatives claim he was severely beaten by officers after his arrest on suspicion of unlawful possession of a firearm.  They say he was restrained for over an hour before being taken to a nearby hospital, where he was pronounced dead.

Police officials denied any misconduct, stating that Khalid was detained for a routine investigation and that no injuries were reported.  The Ministry of Interior has opened an internal inquiry and ordered a forensic examination of the scene and the body.  Human rights groups have called for an independent probe, citing similar incidents in the region where detainees have reportedly suffered abuse.

The case has reignited concerns over the treatment of detainees in Syria’s security system.  Authorities are expected to release the findings of the investigation within the next week, while Khalid’s family has requested a full public review of the circumstances surrounding his death.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Brazil President Calls Amazon Oil a Future Passport
content:
Brazil’s president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, described the recent oil discovery in the Amazon basin as a “passport to the future,” emphasizing the find’s potential to bolster the nation’s economy and reduce reliance on imported energy. The comment was made during a press conference in Manaus following the announcement by state‑run Petrobras that the new field could contain several hundred million barrels of recoverable oil.

Petrobras estimates that production could begin as early as 2027, generating billions of reais in revenue and creating thousands of jobs in the region. The government plans to develop the site under a framework that includes environmental monitoring, compliance with indigenous land rights, and investment in local infrastructure. While officials highlight the project’s contribution to fiscal consolidation and energy security, environmental groups have warned of possible deforestation, biodiversity loss, and increased greenhouse‑gas emissions, urging strict oversight.

Lula’s remarks signal the administration’s intent to integrate the Amazon oil find into Brazil’s broader growth strategy while navigating the attendant ecological and social challenges. The development of the field is expected to become a key element of the country’s energy policy and economic planning in the coming years.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Israeli airstrikes damage Idlib airbase, no casualties reported
content:
Syrian state television reported on Tuesday that Israeli forces conducted an attack in the country, according to a source within the Syrian military. The statement, relayed by the broadcaster, indicated that the strike resulted in material damage but did not cause any fatalities or injuries among civilians or military personnel.

The incident adds to a series of cross‑border confrontations that have marked the volatile relationship between Damascus and Jerusalem in recent months. While the specific target and the extent of the damage were not disclosed, officials in Damascus have previously attributed similar operations to Israel, citing retaliatory motives linked to regional security dynamics. No further details or responses from Israeli authorities were available at the time of reporting.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Exercise-released molecule shown to protect muscles in type 2 diabetes
content:
Scientists have identified a molecule released during physical activity that appears to enhance muscle strength, boost exercise performance, and may offer a new therapeutic avenue for muscle damage associated with type 2 diabetes. The compound, produced by skeletal muscle cells in response to contraction, was shown in laboratory studies to stimulate pathways that increase protein synthesis and improve muscle endurance.

In controlled experiments, animals treated with the molecule exhibited stronger, more resilient muscles and demonstrated higher performance in endurance tests compared to untreated controls. Researchers also observed that the compound mitigated the decline in muscle mass and function typically seen in diabetic models, suggesting it could counteract the catabolic effects of chronic high blood sugar on muscle tissue.

If these findings translate to humans, the molecule could become a novel treatment for preventing or reversing muscle wasting in people with type 2 diabetes, a condition that often leads to reduced mobility and quality of life. Further clinical trials will be necessary to confirm safety and efficacy in patients.
author: Medical Xpress

title: UK trial uses AI to cut aircraft contrail formation
content:
A new United Kingdom trial aims to cut the amount of condensation trails—commonly known as contrails—left by aircraft, a key source of atmospheric heat retention. The pilot project, launched by the UK’s Department for Transport in partnership with the Royal Aeronautical Society, will test a suite of mitigation technologies on a selected fleet of regional jets over the next 18 months.

The trial will deploy advanced engine‑bypass‑air cooling systems, low‑emission fuel blends, and real‑time contrail‑prediction software to adjust flight paths and altitudes. Engineers will monitor changes in contrail formation and persistence using ground‑based lidar and satellite data, comparing the results against a control group of aircraft operating under standard procedures. The goal is to quantify how much the new measures can reduce the radiative forcing associated with contrails, potentially lowering the aviation sector’s contribution to climate change.

If successful, the project could provide a scalable framework for airlines across the UK and beyond, offering a practical step toward meeting the aviation industry’s net‑zero targets. The findings will be published by the end of 2027, informing future regulatory standards and encouraging broader adoption of contrail‑mitigation strategies.
author: BBC Technology
